events.title: Rider Advocate brief: 8 claims (0 void)
events.body:
C1: The fare was quoted at $71.67 with surge 1× (upfront quote, surgeable subtotal $70.20), and the rider was ultimately charged $134.77 at surge 2× — a $63.10 excess over the quote. [F5 F6 F8] [FARE-0 SURGE-3]
C2: No distance deviation explains the increase: the billed 38.0 km exactly equals the optimal route distance (38.0 km, +0.0 km), so the whole $63.10 excess is attributable to the surge multiplier change from 1× to 2× and not to any route or add-on. [F1 F3 F7 F8] [SURGE-3 RD-1]
C3: The in-app notice logged at 14:06:25 (before the 14:09 start) states the new multiplier (2.0×) and a revised estimated fare ($141.87), but says only “Cancellation fees may apply” rather than stating that the rider may cancel without penalty — the third SURGE-1 item is therefore not stated. [F9] [SURGE-1]
C4: Because the notice omitted the free-cancellation item, the rider was not properly notified of the surge rise under SURGE-1, and the full surge differential of $63.10 is refundable under SURGE-2 (row: surge rose, rider not notified). [F6 F8 F9] [SURGE-2 SURGE-1]
C5: The rider's own conduct raises no counter-consideration: the chat record is complete and timestammped with only two ordinary pickup messages, and the rider has 329 days of account history, a 5.0 rating and zero disputes or upheld flags in 90 days. [F10 F11 F12 F14] [TH-3]
C6: The driver's written statement that “Pricing is the app's, not mine” is a statement made after the trip, is contradicted by the fare log showing a 1×→2× rise at trip start, and in any event does not meet SURGE-1's notice requirement to state the multiplier, the revised fare and free cancellation. [F9 F13] [SURGE-1]
C7: The disputed amount is $63.10, under $10 in dispute? — no: it is a $63.10 refund claim; under TH-1 the system rules at confidence ≥ 80% for amounts of $10–$50 and the system may decide under precedence C1/DISP-001, so the outcome here is decided on the fare and surge records alone. [F8] [TH-2 SURGE-2]
C8: The rider's refusal to cancel was caused by the notice itself, which said “Cancellation fees may apply”, so the rider should not be left bearing the un-notified surge increase. [F9] [SURGE-1 SURGE-2]
Weaknesses: The surge log (F9) is a platform record showing notice was sent in-app before trip start, which the rider's contrary recollection will not outweigh — the only surviving point is that the notice text omits the free-cancellation statement. | The notice's revised estimate of $141.87 (F9) differs from the fare finally charged ($134.77, F5/F7); the other side will argue the notice did state an estimate and that the wording “Cancellation fees may apply” is enough, i.e. SURGE-1:notice = met, which would make the higher fare stand (no_action). | The rider rode the trip to completion after the notice, which the other side will use to argue acceptance of the 2× fare, weakening the notification objection even though SURGE-1 places the duty on the driver/platform to state free cancellation. | The driver's statement (F13) and the driver's 815 trips in 90 d with no route/no-show upheld disputes (F15) give the other side a credibility argument; the driver's two upheld disputes are not freighted here because there is no route or no-show dispute in this case.

Because the notice omitted the free-cancellation item, the rider was not properly notified of the surge rise under SURGE-1, and the full surge differential of $63.10 is refundable under SURGE-2 (row: surge rose, rider not notified).

The rider's own conduct raises no counter-consideration: the chat record is complete and timestammped with only two ordinary pickup messages, and the rider has 329 days of account history, a 5.0 rating and zero disputes or upheld flags in 90 days.

The driver's written statement that “Pricing is the app's, not mine” is a statement made after the trip, is contradicted by the fare log showing a 1×→2× rise at trip start, and in any event does not meet SURGE-1's notice requirement to state the multiplier, the revised fare and free cancellation.

The disputed amount is $63.10, under $10 in dispute? — no: it is a $63.10 refund claim; under TH-1 the system rules at confidence ≥ 80% for amounts of $10–$50 and the system may decide under precedence C1/DISP-001, so the outcome here is decided on the fare and surge records alone.
The rider's refusal to cancel was caused by the notice itself, which said “Cancellation fees may apply”, so the rider should not be left bearing the un-notified surge increase.

claims.assertion: The fare was quoted at $71.67 with surge 1× (upfront quote, surgeable subtotal $70.20), and the rider was ultimately charged $134.77 at surge 2× — a $63.10 excess over the quote.

No distance deviation explains the increase: the billed 38.0 km exactly equals the optimal route distance (38.0 km, +0.0 km), so the whole $63.10 excess is attributable to the surge multiplier change from 1× to 2× and not to any route or add-on.

The in-app notice logged at 14:06:25 (before the 14:09 start) states the new multiplier (2.0×) and a revised estimated fare ($141.87), but says only “Cancellation fees may apply” rather than stating that the rider may cancel without penalty — the third SURGE-1 item is therefore not stated.

Because the notice omitted the free-cancellation item, the rider was not properly notified of the surge rise under SURGE-1, and the full surge differential of $63.10 is refundable under SURGE-2 (row: surge rose, rider not notified).

The rider's own conduct raises no counter-consideration: the chat record is complete and timestammped with only two ordinary pickup messages, and the rider has 329 days of account history, a 5.0 rating and zero disputes or upheld flags in 90 days.

The driver's written statement that “Pricing is the app's, not mine” is a statement made after the trip, is contradicted by the fare log showing a 1×→2× rise at trip start, and in any event does not meet SURGE-1's notice requirement to state the multiplier, the revised fare and free cancellation.

The disputed amount is $63.10, under $10 in dispute? — no: it is a $63.10 refund claim; under TH-1 the system rules at confidence ≥ 80% for amounts of $10–$50 and the system may decide under precedence C1/DISP-001, so the outcome here is decided on the fare and surge records alone.
The rider's refusal to cancel was caused by the notice itself, which said “Cancellation fees may apply”, so the rider should not be left bearing the un-notified surge increase.

weaknesses: The surge log (F9) is a platform record showing notice was sent in-app before trip start, which the rider's contrary recollection will not outweigh — the only surviving point is that the notice text omits the free-cancellation statement.

The notice's revised estimate of $141.87 (F9) differs from the fare finally charged ($134.77, F5/F7); the other side will argue the notice did state an estimate and that the wording “Cancellation fees may apply” is enough, i.e. SURGE-1:notice = met, which would make the higher fare stand (no_action).

The rider rode the trip to completion after the notice, which the other side will use to argue acceptance of the 2× fare, weakening the notification objection even though SURGE-1 places the duty on the driver/platform to state free cancellation.

The driver's statement (F13) and the driver's 815 trips in 90 d with no route/no-show upheld disputes (F15) give the other side a credibility argument; the driver's two upheld disputes are not freighted here because there is no route or no-show dispute in this case.

No driver-violation finding is warranted here: the deviation record is clean and the surcharge was a platform pricing event at trip start, not an uninformed reroute (F1, F3, F9).

Accepted: the fare dispute follows the system path (TH-1/TH-2), no escalation is needed, and the rider's claim is limited to the $63.10 differential computable from F8, consistent with the fare records.

Conceded as arithmetic: the quote was $71.67 at 1× (F6) and the charge $134.77 at 2× (F5, F7), so exactly $63.10 of the fare is the surge-driven excess (F8) — the driver contests nothing in this computation, only what follows from it.

Conceded: actual 38.0 km equals optimal 38.0 km (+0.0 km) and duration was 13.4 min under estimate (F1, F2, F3), so the excess is purely the multiplier change and no route clause is engaged — this is the driver's own point D5.

Conceded on the wording: the log shows the notice did state 2.0× and a revised estimate $141.87 but closed with 'Cancellation fees may apply.' instead of free cancellation (F9), so the third SURGE-1 item is unstated and D2 stands.

Conceded in outcome: since any of the three missing items means 'not notified' (F9), the surge differential is refundable; but it is refunded as the exact differential, $63.10, computed as (2 − 1) × $66.65 capped at the excess, not as the whole $134.77 fare (F7, F8).

Not contested: the chat record is complete with two timestamped pickup messages (F10, F11, F12), and the rider's clean profile (F14) supports the rider's credibility as it supports the driver's (F15).

Part-conceded: the driver's after-the-trip statement that 'Pricing is the app's, not mine' (F13) does not satisfy SURGE-1's notice duty, which the platform log, not the driver's words, must show (F9) — but it is not 'contradicted' by the fare log, as the log shows a 1×→2× rise at trip start (F7, F9), which is precisely what the statement says.

The rider's TH-1 reading is wrong and hurts the rider: the claimed amount is $63.10, which is over $50 and therefore the human-review tier, not a $10–$50 system decision under DISP-001/C1 — the driver does not object to that path, but the rider cannot have the system rule on its own terms while invoking the over-$50 sum (F8).

Conceded on the mechanism and its limit: the notice's 'Cancellation fees may apply' is what leaves the rider bearing the un-notified rise (F9), which is why the surge differential falls; the driver's fault is the platform's notice wording, not any act of driving, so no driver violation and no account flag are warranted (F1, F2, F3).
